2.text: often hampered while on the road by the breaking-up of the ice. In order

3.text: to cross the mountain rivers, suddenly swollen by floods, they sometimes

4.text: construct a peculiar device, consisting of several sledges tied together in a

5.text: pile, and protected from beneath by the cover of the outer tent. This is used

6.text: as a raft to carry over men and household things.¹

7.text: HUNTING OF LAND-GAME. — Of land-game, the wild reindeer is the most

8.text: important. It is nevertheless not so abundant in northeastern Asia as the

9.text: caribou in America, because the best pastures are occupied by domesticated

10.text: herds. Only the depths of the forests and the higher slopes of the mountains

11.text: are left quite undisturbed for the wild breed, because they are unsuitable for

12.text: the breeding of domesticated animals. Wild reindeer, however, are met every-

13.text: where in northeastern Asia, in single heads or in small herds.

14.text: The wild reindeer is larger than any of the domesticated varieties. Its

15.text: step is wider, and its footprint longer, because its hoof-joints are more supple.

16.text: Its antlers are more or less similar to those of the Lamut reindeer, but generally

17.text: the ends are bent up in a hook-like shape. Also the difference in size of

18.text: antlers between buck and doe is still more marked than with Lamut reindeer.

19.text: The color of the skin is uniformly dark gray, somewhat lighter on the belly

20.text: and lower part of the neck. Those living on the northeastern tundras and

21.text: close to the ocean are smaller, but accumulate more fat. In this respect,

22.text: however, all varieties of the wild reindeer are superior, even to the Chukchee

23.text: breed. Late in summer, when insects cease to swarm around the pastures, a

24.text: wild buck often takes on three inches of tallow on his hips, so that he is no

25.text: longer able to run with his usual swiftness.

26.text: Some wild reindeer always live in the same places. They are called

27.text: “resident reindeer.” Others gather every year in large herds and migrate

28.text: considerable distances, from the forest border to the tundra and back again.

29.text: In former times there were two different trails in northeastern Asia for

30.text: these migrations. One led from the Kolyma Mountains across the Omolon

31.text: and the two Anui Rivers to the Chaun tundra; the other, from the high

32.text: country of Palpal, across the Anadyr River, to the Chukchee Peninsula. About

33.text: fourscore years ago the reindeer migration over the former trail began to lessen,

34.text: and finally ceased altogether. Several Yukaghir villages which depended on

35.text: wild reindeer for their subsistence were starved out in consequence, and the

36.text: remainder went to the northwest and settled in the Russo-Yukaghir fishing-

37.text: villages on the Kolyma River. In the year 1896, when descending the Omolon

38.text: on a raft, I passed several of these deserted or starved-out hamlets. The

39.text: houses of some were still standing. Others had completely fallen in, and only

40.text: a grassy patch that interrupted the continuous line of the forest along the

41.text: bank indicated the former dwelling-place of humanity. For the abandonment
